content.comment_body: Since buying new devices wasn't an option, I decided to purchase three used [product_name] modules from an online auction; one with article number [article_no] and two with article number [article_no]. The device with firmware [version_no] works as expected, but I'm concerned that the other two may be defective and am exploring ways they can be restored. It's possible I'm missing something in the process. When powering up one of the potentially faulty modules, there is no response—no display or backlight. The other unit powers the backlight but shows no content on the LCD and is unresponsive to button presses. Connecting to the LAN port on each device causes the LED to illuminate, but [product_name] software fails to establish a connection. I attempted the recommended reset procedure using the __reset.bm file on an SD card, but it had no effect. Are there any further steps I could take to recover these modules, such as firmware flashing or other methods?

The module with firmware version [version_no] matches [product_name] [version_no]. The other two units ([article_no]) are [product_name] [version_no] modules. The Reset Tool only works for [product_name] [version_no] devices. If applying the supply voltage results in no display or activity, it's likely these two modules are defective.

I'm relieved—the solution was simple in the end. I refused to accept the devices were irreparably damaged, so I inspected them closely. The LCD ribbon cables in both units were loose and not latched, so I reconnected them and, after powering up, both modules functioned perfectly. Very glad for the outcome!
It's unusual for two modules to exhibit the identical problem of a loose connector. This might indicate prior intentional tampering.

I concur. The only innocent explanation might be that both devices experienced a hard impact that dislodged the ribbons. Yet, with the locking tab open on both, it's unlikely they would still operate at all if this happened. Regardless, I now have three working modules instead of just one.
From the two provided pictures, it seems the modules weren't dropped. On the left, the locking lever is visibly open, which wouldn't result from dropping the devices.
It appears there's an interest in creating versions of these controllers without displays.

analysis.insight_summary: Users ran into problems with secondhand [product_name] hardware modules, initially believing them to be permanently faulty. After investigating, they realized that unattached LCD ribbon cables were the cause and, once reconnected, the devices functioned correctly. This situation showcased the sensitivity of internal connections to physical handling and emphasized the importance of checking for such issues. Additionally, confusion emerged due to trying software tools designed for incompatible module versions, revealing the need for better guidance regarding compatibility.
analysis.user_expectations: The user hopes that the secondhand [product_name] modules will work reliably or be restorable using diagnostic software or firmware updates. Guidance is sought for reviving modules that do not respond and for understanding whether recovery is possible.
